drugs.name: Infliximab (Remicade/Avsola/Inflectra/Flixabi)
drugs.mechanism: Chimeric mouse-human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody (75% human, 25% murine); binds both soluble and membrane-bound TNF with high affinity, neutralizing signaling through TNFR1/TNFR2 and inducing apoptosis of TNF-expressing immune cells via Fc-mediated CDC and ADCC
drugs.approval: FDA approved 1998 (CD). Also approved for UC (2005). First biologic approved for IBD. Must be combined with baseline therapy.
drugs.route: IV infusion at weeks 0, 2, 6 (induction), then every 8 weeks (maintenance)
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~60-70% in CD (ACCENT I trial); ~65-70% in UC (ACT trials). Mucosal healing in ~45% at 1 year. Reduces surgery and hospitalization rates.

drugs.name: Adalimumab (Humira/Hyrimoz/Cyltezo)
drugs.mechanism: Fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody binding soluble and membrane-bound TNF; blocks TNFR1/TNFR2-mediated inflammation, leukocyte recruitment, and matrix metalloproteinase production in the gut mucosa
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2007 (CD), 2012 (UC). Most widely prescribed biologic globally. Subcutaneous self-administration at home.
drugs.route: Subcutaneous injection; induction 160/80 mg at weeks 0/2, then 40 mg every 2 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~35-45% in CD (CLASSIC-I/CHARM). Clinical response ~50% in UC (ULTRA trials). ~40% mucosal healing at 1 year.

drugs.name: Certolizumab Pegol (Cimzia)
drugs.mechanism: PEGylated humanized anti-TNF Fab fragment (no Fc region); neutralizes both soluble and membrane-bound TNF without inducing CDC or ADCC. PEGylation extends half-life and may improve tissue penetration. Minimal placental transfer.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2008 (CD). Not approved for UC. Only anti-TNF suitable for use throughout pregnancy (minimal placental FcRn-mediated transfer).
drugs.route: Subcutaneous injection; 400 mg at weeks 0, 2, 4 (induction), then every 4 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~37-40% in moderate-severe CD (PRECiSE trials). Maintenance of remission ~48% at 26 weeks. Preferred in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Golimumab (Simponi)
drugs.mechanism: Fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody with high affinity and conformational stability; neutralizes soluble and transmembrane TNF, inhibiting downstream NF-κB and MAP kinase signaling in intestinal immune cells
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2013 (UC). Not approved for CD. Monthly maintenance dosing after subcutaneous induction.
drugs.route: Subcutaneous injection; 200/100 mg at weeks 0/2, then 100 mg every 4 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~55% and remission ~18% at week 6 (PURSUIT-SC). Sustained remission ~28% at week 54 (PURSUIT-M).

drugs.name: Vedolizumab (Entyvio)
drugs.mechanism: Humanized anti-α4β7 integrin monoclonal antibody that selectively blocks MAdCAM-1 binding on gut-homing T lymphocytes, preventing their extravasation into intestinal mucosa without affecting systemic immune surveillance. Gut-selective: does not block α4β1-VCAM-1 (unlike natalizumab).
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2014 (CD and UC). First gut-selective biologic. Preferred first-line biologic in many guidelines for moderate-severe UC and CD.
drugs.route: IV infusion at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks. Subcutaneous formulation approved 2023.
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~47% in UC (GEMINI I) and ~31% in CD (GEMINI II/III) at week 6. Superior to adalimumab for UC in VARSITY trial. Mucosal healing ~43% in UC at 1 year.

drugs.name: Ustekinumab (Stelara)
drugs.mechanism: Fully human anti-IL-12/IL-23 p40 monoclonal antibody; blocks both IL-12 (Th1) and IL-23 (Th17) pathways simultaneously. Prevents IL-12 interaction with IL-12Rβ1 and IL-23 interaction with IL-23R/IL-12Rβ1.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2016 (CD), 2019 (UC). First anti-IL-12/23 biologic in IBD. IV induction followed by SC maintenance.
drugs.route: Single IV induction dose (weight-based), then subcutaneous every 8 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~40% in CD (UNITI-1). Remission ~53% in UC (UNIFI) at 1 year. Effective in anti-TNF failures. Histologic remission superior to placebo.

drugs.name: Risankizumab (Skyrizi)
drugs.mechanism: Humanized anti-IL-23 p19 monoclonal antibody; selectively blocks IL-23 without affecting IL-12, preserving Th1 immunity against intracellular pathogens. Targets the p19 subunit unique to IL-23.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2022 (CD). Pivotal UC trials ongoing. Selective IL-23 blockade with potential safety advantages over p40 inhibition.
drugs.route: IV induction at weeks 0, 4, 8, then subcutaneous every 8 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~45% in CD at week 12 (ADVANCE/MOTIVATE). Endoscopic response ~40% at week 12. Superior to ustekinumab in head-to-head CD trial (SEQUENCE).

drugs.name: Mirikizumab (Omvoh)
drugs.mechanism: Humanized anti-IL-23 p19 monoclonal antibody; selectively neutralizes IL-23-driven Th17 and innate lymphoid cell (ILC3) responses in the colonic mucosa, reducing IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22 production
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2023 (UC). Also in development for CD. First IL-23 p19 inhibitor approved for UC.
drugs.route: IV induction at weeks 0, 4, 8, then subcutaneous every 4 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~24% vs 13% placebo at week 12 (LUCENT-1). Histologic-endoscopic mucosal remission ~27% at week 12. Sustained remission ~50% at 1 year (LUCENT-2).

drugs.name: Tofacitinib (Xeljanz)
drugs.mechanism: Oral JAK inhibitor preferentially targeting JAK1 and JAK3; blocks signaling downstream of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 (common gamma chain), type I IFN, and IL-6 family cytokine receptors in mucosal immune cells
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2018 (UC). Not approved for CD (negative phase II trials). First oral small molecule for moderate-severe UC. JAK inhibitor class carries FDA black box warning for cardiovascular and malignancy risk.
drugs.route: Oral, 10 mg twice daily (induction), then 5 mg twice daily (maintenance)
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~18.5% vs 8.2% placebo at week 8 (OCTAVE Induction). Sustained remission ~34% at 1 year (OCTAVE Sustain). Rapid onset within 3 days. Effective in anti-TNF failures.

drugs.name: Upadacitinib (Rinvoq)
drugs.mechanism: Oral selective JAK1 inhibitor engineered for JAK1 selectivity over JAK2/JAK3/TYK2; blocks IL-6, type I/II IFN, IL-10 family, and common gamma chain cytokine signaling with minimal hematologic impact from JAK2 sparing
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2022 (UC), 2023 (CD). First JAK inhibitor approved for Crohn's disease. Once-daily oral dosing.
drugs.route: Oral, 45 mg once daily (induction 8-12 weeks), then 15 mg or 30 mg once daily (maintenance)
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~26-33% in UC at week 8 (U-ACHIEVE/U-ACCOMPLISH). ~36-49% endoscopic response in CD at week 12 (U-EXCEED/U-EXCEL). Superior to placebo in both anti-TNF naive and experienced.

drugs.name: Ozanimod (Zeposia)
drugs.mechanism: Oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator with selectivity for S1PR1 and S1PR5; induces internalization and degradation of S1PR1 on lymphocytes, sequestering them in lymph nodes and preventing egress into the intestinal mucosa. Short half-life allows rapid lymphocyte recovery.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2021 (UC). First S1P receptor modulator approved for IBD. Dose titration required to avoid first-dose bradycardia.
drugs.route: Oral, 7-day dose titration from 0.23 mg to 0.92 mg once daily
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~18.4% vs 6% placebo at week 10 (True North induction). Sustained remission ~37% at week 52. Endoscopic improvement ~27% at week 10.

drugs.name: Etrasimod (Velsipity)
drugs.mechanism: Oral selective S1PR1/4/5 modulator with no activity at S1PR3 (reducing cardiovascular risk). Internalizes lymphocyte S1PR1, preventing their egress from lymph nodes and Peyer's patches into the systemic circulation and gut mucosa. Short half-life (~30 hours) allows rapid immune reconstitution.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2023 (UC). Second-generation S1P modulator with improved safety profile. No first-dose monitoring required (no S1PR3-mediated bradycardia).
drugs.route: Oral, 2 mg once daily (no titration required)
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~27% vs 7% placebo at week 12 (ELEVATE UC 12). ~32% at week 52. Endoscopic improvement ~41% at week 12. Effective regardless of prior biologic exposure.

drugs.name: Natalizumab (Tysabri)
drugs.mechanism: Humanized anti-α4 integrin monoclonal antibody blocking both α4β1 (VLA-4) and α4β7 integrins; prevents lymphocyte binding to VCAM-1 (systemic) and MAdCAM-1 (gut), broadly inhibiting leukocyte trafficking into the CNS and GI tract
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2008 (CD). Restricted use due to risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Requires TOUCH prescribing program. Only used in anti-TNF refractory patients with negative JC virus serology.
drugs.route: IV infusion every 4 weeks
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~56% at week 12 (ENACT-1). Sustained remission ~44% at week 36 (ENACT-2). Highly effective but reserved for refractory CD due to PML risk increasing with JC virus seropositivity and duration >2 years.

drugs.name: Azathioprine (Imuran/Azasan)
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine then to 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN); incorporates into DNA as fraudulent nucleotide, inhibiting purine synthesis and selectively suppressing proliferating T and B lymphocytes. TPMT genotyping recommended before initiation.
drugs.approval: FDA approved (CD and UC). Traditional immunomodulator for steroid-sparing maintenance. Largely replaced by biologics. Still used as combination therapy or monotherapy in resource-limited settings.
drugs.route: Oral, 2-2.5 mg/kg/day (TPMT-adjusted)
drugs.efficacy: Maintains steroid-free remission in ~50-60% of IBD patients. Slower onset (8-12 weeks). Reduces surgical recurrence in CD. Inferior to infliximab monotherapy in SONIC trial. Higher lymphoma risk with long-term use.

drugs.name: 6-Mercaptopurine (Purinethol)
drugs.mechanism: Thiopurine antimetabolite converted intracellularly to 6-thioguanine nucleotides that incorporate into DNA and inhibit de novo purine synthesis; suppresses lymphocyte proliferation and induces T cell apoptosis in the intestinal mucosa
drugs.approval: FDA approved (CD and UC). Classic immunomodulator; active metabolite of azathioprine. Preferentially used when azathioprine intolerance due to GI side effects.
drugs.route: Oral, 1-1.5 mg/kg/day (TPMT-adjusted)
drugs.efficacy: Comparable to azathioprine for maintenance of remission. 6-TGN levels >235 pmol/8×10^8 RBC correlate with efficacy. Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and NUDT15 testing recommended to prevent leukopenia.

drugs.name: Methotrexate (Rheumatrex/Trexall/Otrexup)
drugs.mechanism: Folate antagonist inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase and AICAR transformylase, leading to adenosine accumulation with anti-inflammatory effects; suppresses T cell activation, neutrophil chemotaxis, and pro-inflammatory cytokine production
drugs.approval: FDA approved (CD). Off-label for UC. Second-line immunomodulator for CD. Preferred over thiopurines in some patients due to lower lymphoma risk.
drugs.route: Subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, 15-25 mg weekly (higher bioavailability than oral). Oral also available.
drugs.efficacy: Clinical remission ~39% vs 19% placebo at week 16 in steroid-dependent CD (FEAGAN trial). Maintains remission in ~65% at 40 weeks. Requires folic acid supplementation.

drugs.name: Mesalamine / 5-ASA (Asacol/Lialda/Pentasa/Apriso/Delzicol)
drugs.mechanism: Topical anti-inflammatory aminosalicylate acting locally on the colonic mucosa; activates PPAR-γ, inhibits NF-κB, COX-2, and lipoxygenase pathways, and scavenges reactive oxygen species. Various formulations provide delayed-release delivery to different GI segments.
drugs.approval: FDA approved (UC). First-line for mild-moderate UC induction and maintenance. Not effective as monotherapy for CD (negative meta-analyses). Also used for microscopic colitis and pouchitis.
drugs.route: Oral (various delayed-release formulations) and/or rectal (enema/suppository). Combined oral + rectal superior to either alone.
drugs.efficacy: Induces clinical remission in ~35-45% of mild-moderate UC at 8 weeks. Reduces UC relapse by ~40-50% at 1 year maintenance. Maintains remission post-UC colectomy (pouchitis prevention). Chemopreventive against colorectal cancer.

drugs.name: Budesonide (Entocort/Budesonide MMX/Uceris)
drugs.mechanism: Oral corticosteroid with high first-pass hepatic metabolism (~90%); high topical glucocorticoid potency on intestinal mucosa with minimal systemic bioavailability. Enteric-coated formulations target ileum and ascending colon (CD) or entire colon (UC MMX).
drugs.approval: FDA approved (CD - Entocort; UC - Uceris/MMX). First-line corticosteroid for mild-moderate ileocecal CD. Superior safety profile to prednisone. Not effective for severe or colonic CD.
drugs.route: Oral, 9 mg once daily (induction), tapering to 3-6 mg
drugs.efficacy: Induces remission in ~50-60% of mild-moderate ileocecal CD at 8 weeks. Less effective than prednisone for severe disease. Minimal HPA axis suppression compared to prednisone. Does not prevent long-term relapse as maintenance.

drugs.name: Prednisone/Prednisolone
drugs.mechanism: Systemic glucocorticoid binding to cytoplasmic GR leads to nuclear translocation, transrepression of pro-inflammatory genes (AP-1, NF-κB) and transactivation of anti-inflammatory genes (annexin-1, IL-10). Broadly suppresses intestinal and systemic inflammation.
drugs.approval: Standard of care for moderate-severe IBD flares. Rapid onset bridge therapy while initiating immunomodulators or biologics. Long-term use avoided due to toxicity.
drugs.route: Oral, 40-60 mg daily (tapered over 8-12 weeks). IV methylprednisolone for severe hospitalized UC.
drugs.efficacy: Induces remission in ~50-80% of moderate-severe UC and CD within 2-4 weeks. Does not maintain long-term remission. 1-year steroid-free remission without biologics/immunomodulators only ~30%. Significant toxicity with prolonged use.

drugs.name: Cyclosporine A (Neoral/Sandimmune)
drugs.mechanism: Calcineurin inhibitor forming complex with cyclophilin A to block NFAT dephosphorylation, inhibiting IL-2 transcription and T cell activation. High-dose IV cyclosporine is a rescue therapy for severe steroid-refractory UC.
drugs.approval: Off-label for severe steroid-refractory UC. Bridge therapy to avoid emergency colectomy. Narrow therapeutic window requiring drug level monitoring.
drugs.route: IV, 2-4 mg/kg/day continuous infusion (inpatient), then transition to oral 5-8 mg/kg/day. Trough levels 300-400 ng/mL (IV), 150-300 ng/mL (oral).
drugs.efficacy: Initial response ~60-80% in severe steroid-refractory UC within 7 days. Colectomy-free survival ~50-60% at 1 year when bridged to thiopurines. Comparable 7-day efficacy to infliximab (CYSIF trial). Limited by nephrotoxicity and hypertension.

drugs.name: Tacrolimus (Prograf/FK506)
drugs.mechanism: Calcineurin inhibitor binding FKBP12 to inhibit calcineurin phosphatase activity, blocking NFAT translocation and IL-2 gene transcription; suppresses T cell activation in the colonic mucosa. Topical rectal formulation also effective.
drugs.approval: Off-label for refractory UC and perianal CD. Alternative to cyclosporine for severe UC with more predictable oral bioavailability. Used as bridge to thiopurines or vedolizumab.
drugs.route: Oral, 0.1-0.2 mg/kg/day (target trough 10-15 ng/mL initial, 5-10 ng/mL maintenance). Topical rectal ointment also available for distal disease.
drugs.efficacy: Clinical response ~50-70% in moderate-severe refractory UC at 2 weeks. Colectomy-free rate ~60-70% at 12 weeks. Comparable efficacy to cyclosporine with fewer serious adverse events in some meta-analyses.
